title: The Patient House
premise: Edmund Coldharbour, a hospice nurse who hears the dying count backwards, inherits his grandmother's house and discovers that every photograph taken inside it now contains an empty chair that draws the eye — and then the people. The house was built by founders who bound a hungry presence into its walls, sustained by a ritual of substitution: a chair for a life. As Edmund's family is pulled one by one toward the chair, he must choose between finishing the founders' ritual by sacrificing an outsider or unmaking it entirely, knowing his own backwards-counting patients were all former keepers who refused. In the end Edmund sits in the chair himself, offering not a life but his disbelief, and the house — finally believed in — lets go.
about_author: Odile Whitlock spent a decade as a night-shift caregiver before turning to writing, and her fiction is shaped by the hushed hours of hospice wards. She lives in a drafty Victorian house she insists is perfectly ordinary, thank you very much.

chapters.title: The Counting Ward
chapters.summary: Edmund, POV, tends a dying patient who counts backwards from ten without ever reaching zero, as every terminal patient at Marrow Hospice seems to do. He documents it clinically, refusing superstition. Emotional beat: quiet unease masked by professional detachment.

chapters.title: Letters from a House That Waits
chapters.summary: Edmund receives notice of his grandmother Agnes's death and her bequest: the Coldharbour house on Vesper Lane. His sister Ruth begs him to sell it unseen; their mother went silent years ago after visiting. POV Edmund. Beat: dread disguised as inheritance paperwork.

chapters.title: The Photograph Problem
chapters.summary: Sorting Agnes's belongings, Edmund notices every photo of the parlor now includes an extra wooden chair no one remembers — including photos from 1962. Ruth photographs the room; the chair appears in the new shot, closer. POV alternating Edmund/Ruth. Beat: denial cracking.

chapters.title: What Agnes Kept Under the Floorboards
chapters.summary: Edmund finds Agnes's journal beneath the pantry: accounts of 'the Founders,' a ledger of names crossed out, and the phrase 'the house must be fed by consent.' He reads it as grief-madness. POV Edmund. Beat: first real fear, still rationalized.

chapters.title: The Chair Moves
chapters.summary: Ruth stays overnight; by morning the chair stands at the foot of her bed, facing her. She flees to a motel, but the chair appears in a photo texted from her phone she never took. POV Ruth. Beat: terror arrives; the house follows them now.

chapters.title: The Founder's Descendant
chapters.summary: Edmund tracks down Silas Marn, elderly descendant of the house's builders, who confirms the ritual: a keeper feeds the house a life each generation, or it takes freely. Silas's own family line ended badly. POV Edmund. Beat: the supernatural becomes documented fact.

chapters.title: Backwards From Ten
chapters.summary: A hospice patient grabs Edmund's wrist and counts down, then whispers: 'Agnes counted too. Ask what number she stopped at.' Edmund checks the journal — Agnes's last entry ends mid-count. POV Edmund. Beat: personal history revealed as warning.

chapters.title: Ruth Is Called
chapters.summary: Ruth begins sleepwalking back toward Vesper Lane, waking miles away with splinters in her palms. The chair has begun appearing in mirrors behind her. POV Ruth. Beat: the hunt narrows; helplessness sets in.

chapters.title: The Ritual of Substitution
chapters.summary: Silas explains the mechanics: the chair must be filled willingly by a keeper, or the house chooses among blood. The founders bound it to protect the town from something worse underneath. POV Edmund. Beat: moral horror — survival requires sacrifice.

chapters.title: Mother's Silence
chapters.summary: Edmund visits their mother, Marion, in a care facility; she has been counting backwards for twenty years, a failed keeper. She recognizes him only long enough to say: 'Don't sit down.' POV Edmund. Beat: generational wound exposed.

chapters.title: The House Opens
chapters.summary: Edmund returns to prepare the ritual and finds doors rearranged, rooms looping, walls breathing faintly. The house is awake and impatient. He hears counting through the floorboards — many voices. POV Edmund. Beat: claustrophobic escalation.

chapters.title: An Outsider's Price
chapters.summary: Silas offers a solution: lure a stranger — a drifter, a dying volunteer — to fill the chair instead. Edmund, a nurse sworn to protect the vulnerable, recoils. POV Edmund. Beat: ethical crisis; the theme of survival's price made explicit.

chapters.title: Ruth Crosses the Threshold
chapters.summary: Ruth disappears entirely; her car is found idling outside the house. Inside, Edmund finds her seated near the chair, entranced, counting softly. He pulls her out, but she no longer answers to her name. POV Edmund. Beat: stakes become intimate and immediate.

chapters.title: What Sits Beneath
chapters.summary: In the cellar, Edmund finds the original binding: not a demon but a starving thing the founders trapped — and fed — to keep it from the town. The house isn't evil; it's a cage. POV Edmund. Beat: moral inversion, sympathy for the monster.

chapters.title: Silas's Confession
chapters.summary: Silas admits the founders' descendants invented the 'outsider option' generations ago; every keeper who refused became a counter. He urges Edmund to finish it before the house takes Ruth. POV Silas briefly, then Edmund. Beat: betrayal and complicity across generations.

chapters.title: The Empty Chair Fills
chapters.summary: Edmund attempts the ritual with a willing substitute — himself — but the house rejects him: keepers must believe. His lifelong disbelief is the barrier. Ruth, half-lost, begins rising toward the chair. POV Edmund. Beat: climax approach; identity as obstacle.

chapters.title: Counting Forward
chapters.summary: Marion dies at the facility counting — but forward, for the first time, as if passing something on. Edmund understands: belief isn't faith in ghosts, it's accepting what you've witnessed. He accepts everything he's seen. POV Edmund. Beat: transformation.

chapters.title: The Sitting
chapters.summary: Edmund sits in the chair willingly, believing fully, offering himself. The house takes his offering — but not his life: it takes his refusal, his armor of disbelief, leaving him raw and open to everything he'd denied. POV Edmund. Beat: climax and sacrifice.

chapters.title: The House Lets Go
chapters.summary: The chair crumbles to ash; the photographs return to normal; the thing below goes quiet, finally acknowledged rather than starved. Ruth wakes whole, remembering nothing but warmth. POV Ruth. Beat: release and tenderness after horror.

chapters.title: Aftermath at Vesper Lane
chapters.summary: Edmund and Ruth repair the house together. He can now hear the dying clearly — not counting down, but speaking names, messages, goodbyes. His curse has become a gift. POV Edmund. Beat: bittersweet healing.

chapters.title: The Last Keeper
chapters.summary: Silas dies peacefully, counting forward to zero. At the funeral, Edmund realizes the keeping has passed to him — not as burden but as witness. He keeps the journal going, adding truth where Agnes could only record fear. POV Edmund. Beat: inheritance redefined.

chapters.title: Epilogue: Someone New Counts Backwards
chapters.summary: Months later, a new hospice patient counts backwards from ten — and stops at three, smiling at Edmund: 'Yours is a kind house now.' Some things endure; some are changed. Edmund goes home to Vesper Lane, where every photograph holds exactly the right number of chairs. POV Edmund. Beat: resonant, uneasy peace.
